q: Your 406 MHz EPIRB has been switched on. Which system carries its alert to a rescue centre?
a: Cospas-Sarsat satellites
o: NAVTEX coast stations
VHF DSC coast stations
AIS shore stations
why: 406 MHz EPIRBs are detected by the Cospas-Sarsat satellite system, which passes alerts to MRCCs.

q: A lifeboat is closing in on your liferaft, guided by your EPIRB. Which of its signals does she use for the final approach?
a: The 121.5 MHz homing signal
o: The 406 MHz satellite burst
A voice call on channel 16
A 518 kHz NAVTEX signal
why: EPIRBs also send 121.5 MHz so rescuers can home in on them; 406 MHz goes to the satellites.

q: You are buying an EPIRB for the boat. Why choose B?
a: Its position reaches rescuers faster and more precisely
o: It also makes voice calls on channel 16
It works without being registered
It needs no 121.5 MHz homing signal
why: A GPS EPIRB sends its own position in the alert; without GPS the satellites must work it out.

q: You buy a used yacht whose EPIRB is still registered to the previous owner. What do you do?
a: Update the registration with your and the boat's details
o: Nothing — the registration stays with the beacon
Switch it on once so the system learns you
Register it only if you sail offshore
why: Rescuers use the registration to phone the owner and identify the boat: keep it current.

q: What happens to this beacon if the yacht sinks before anyone can reach it?
a: It floats free and switches itself on
o: It stays in its bracket until someone frees it
It sends a DSC alert on channel 70
It sinks with the boat, sealed in its bracket
why: Category I: the hydrostatic release frees it at depth; it floats up and activates automatically.

fig.title: EPIRB on the pushpit
lines: In a bracket with a hydrostatic release

q: At the start of the season you want to check that the EPIRB works. How?
a: Run its self-test, as the maker's manual says
o: Switch it on for a minute and call the coastguard
Drop it in a bucket of water to see it start
Leave it on overnight and see if anyone calls
why: Use only the built-in self-test, per the instructions; a real activation sends a live alert.

q: You find the beacon has been transmitting by accident. What do you do?
a: Switch it off and tell the coastguard / MRCC
o: Switch it off and say nothing — it was brief
Leave it on until the coastguard calls you
Send SEELONCE FEENEE on channel 16
why: A false alert may already be in the system: switch off and inform the coastguard at once.

q: Your yacht has an EPIRB, and a crew member wears a PLB on her lifejacket. What is the key difference?
a: The EPIRB is registered to the boat, the PLB to a person
o: The PLB uses only 121.5 MHz, no satellites
The EPIRB is meant for inland waters only
The PLB works only with a VHF DSC radio
why: Both alert via 406 MHz satellites; the EPIRB identifies the vessel, the PLB a person.

q: You are in the liferaft and switch on the SART. What does it do?
a: Shows as a line of dots on a ship's radar
o: Sends your position to the satellites
Calls nearby ships by voice on 16
Flashes a light seen 10 miles away
why: A SART answers a ship's 9 GHz (X-band) radar and paints a line of 12 dots on its screen.

q: The rescue ship's radar shows this. Where exactly is the SART?
a: At the dot nearest the ship
o: At the dot farthest from the ship
In the middle of the line of dots
Anywhere along the line of dots
why: The SART is at the first dot, the one closest to the ship; the line runs on beyond it.

fig.title: Radar screen
lines: Running outwards, away from the ship

q: Your liferaft carries an AIS-SART instead of a radar SART. Who will see it?
a: Any vessel showing AIS targets
o: Only ships with a 9 GHz radar
Only the Cospas-Sarsat satellites
Only coast stations with NAVTEX
why: An AIS-SART sends AIS messages with its position, shown on any AIS display nearby.

q: You fit a NAVTEX receiver at the chart table. Which frequency does it listen on?
a: 518 kHz
o: 406 MHz
why: International NAVTEX broadcasts go out on 518 kHz, in English.

q: Your NAVTEX prints this header. What does the letter B tell you about the message?
a: It is a meteorological warning
o: It is a navigational warning
It is a routine weather forecast
It is search-and-rescue news
why: The second letter is the subject: A navigational warning, B meteorological warning, D SAR, E forecast.

q: Your NAVTEX prints warnings from stations far from where you sail. How do you limit it to your area?
a: Select the letters of the local stations
o: Tune it to the local station's frequency
Enter the local station's MMSI
Set it to the local VHF channel
why: All stations share 518 kHz; you choose which station letters (and message types) to print.

q: A ferry nearby carries Class A AIS; your yacht has Class B. Which is true?
a: Class B sends less often and at lower power
o: Class B gets priority over A in busy areas
Class B only receives and never transmits
Class A is meant for yachts, B for ships
why: Class A is the ship standard; Class B is a simpler small-craft set with lower power and slower reports.

q: Does this mean the way ahead is clear of other vessels?
a: No — many boats have no AIS; keep a lookout
o: Yes — every vessel must transmit AIS
Yes — within 12 miles of the coast
Yes — only small fishing boats lack AIS
why: AIS is an aid, not a lookout: many craft carry none or have it switched off.

q: Your instructor says GMDSS changed rescue at sea. What is its main idea?
a: Distress alerts reach rescue centres automatically
o: Every yacht must carry a satellite phone
Coast stations no longer listen on VHF
Morse code is used for every distress alert
why: GMDSS: automatic alerting (DSC, EPIRB) so a distress reaches shore even if no one hears a voice call.

q: Which GMDSS sea area are you sailing in?
a: A1
o: A2
A3
A4
why: Sea area A1 is defined by the range of VHF DSC coast stations.

fig.title: Your cruising area
lines: In range of VHF DSC coast stations

q: Your passage takes you 80 miles offshore, beyond the range of VHF DSC coast stations. Which means can still alert a rescue centre from there?
a: A 406 MHz EPIRB, through the satellites
o: VHF DSC on high power — range doubles
The NAVTEX receiver, which sends alerts
AIS Class B, which alerts the MRCC
why: Beyond A1 your VHF will not reach shore; a 406 MHz EPIRB alerts via satellite from anywhere.

q: You are in the liferaft with a radar SART. Where do you put it?
a: As high as possible, on its pole
o: In the water, tied to the raft
Inside the canopy, on the floor
Under the raft, in a ballast pocket
why: SART range depends on height: hold or mount it as high as you can.
